slides.label: Title
slides.notes: Open the lecture by framing this chapter as a capstone rather than a bag of unrelated algorithms. The repeated pattern is that local predicates become global structures, and global structures are only trustworthy when their invariants can be inspected after construction. This sets up the whole deck as a reliability story for graphics geometry.

slides.label: Predicate Contracts
slides.notes: Spend time on this slide because it is the vocabulary for the chapter. A predicate is not just a formula; it is a contract about what sign means, how zero is handled, and which convention is used on boundaries. Algorithms later in the lecture succeed or fail based on these small contracts.

slides.label: BSP Trees
slides.notes: Explain BSP trees as a controlled way to remember a sequence of spatial decisions. The geometric primitive at a node is simple, but the recursion turns many side tests into a spatial index. Emphasize that the danger is not only depth; bad splitters also create duplicated fragments that make later queries expensive.

slides.label: Point Containment
slides.notes: Use this slide to separate the mathematical region from the implementation policy. Parity and winding both answer containment, but they encode different information about orientation and holes. Students should leave knowing that vertex crossings and boundary points are not annoyances to hide; they are part of the API contract.

slides.label: Boolean Operations
slides.notes: Present polygon or solid Booleans as a graph problem induced by geometry. The visible overlapping shapes are only the first step; the real computation is the arrangement whose edges carry inside outside labels. Stress that robustness problems often appear after intersections, when short fragments and coincident pieces must be classified consistently.

slides.label: Convex Hulls
slides.notes: Connect hulls back to the orientation predicate from the beginning. The hull is a global object, but every edge can be checked with local side tests against all input points. This makes the hull a good example of the chapter theme: a data structure should carry a certificate that can be audited.

slides.label: Delaunay Triangulation
slides.notes: Make the contrast with hulls explicit. A hull edge is certified by a support halfspace, while a Delaunay triangle is certified by an empty circle. The flip picture is useful because students can see a local repair: a bad diagonal is not morally bad, it simply violates the circumcircle predicate.

slides.label: Hull And Delaunay Duality
slides.notes: This slide is a synthesis checkpoint. Hulls and Delaunay triangulations can look like different chapters, but both are ways to amplify local predicates into reusable structures. Ask students to name the certificate before naming the algorithm. If they can name the certificate, they can design a check and debug failures.

slides.label: Polygon Partitioning
slides.notes: Describe partitioning as a deliberate change of representation. The original polygon is not discarded; its boundary and area must be recoverable from the pieces. This is a good place to connect algorithms to validation: counting triangles is useful, but area preservation catches many wrong diagonals and orientation errors.

slides.label: Minimum Bounds
slides.notes: Emphasize that bounding primitives are part of the computational geometry toolbox because they sit between exact geometry and fast rejection tests. The minimal rectangle and minimal circle both have small support certificates. In practice, students should distinguish containment correctness from optimality, because a nonminimal bound can still be a valid accelerator.

slides.label: Area And Volume
slides.notes: Treat formulas here as diagnostic instruments, not as isolated facts. Signed area and signed volume both expose orientation decisions. A figure may look right while its vertex order is inconsistent, but a signed sum will usually reveal the inconsistency. This connects measurement back to representation and boundary convention.

slides.label: Robustness
slides.notes: This is the engineering hinge of the lecture. Exact mathematical statements often assume generic position, while graphics data arrives with duplicate vertices, nearly parallel edges, and finite precision arithmetic. The goal is not to scare students away from algorithms; it is to make them specify what happens near zero and test those choices.

slides.label: Graphics Pipeline
slides.notes: Use this slide to translate the chapter into software architecture. A geometry pipeline should not throw away its reasons. When a modeler performs a Boolean operation, or a mesher builds triangles, the later stages need enough state to audit the result. This idea helps students design debuggable tools rather than opaque geometric black boxes.

slides.label: Lab Pattern
slides.notes: Make this slide actionable. The lab is not a request to implement every algorithm in the chapter at full production scale. Instead, students should practice the notebook pattern on a small scene: expose the active geometric feature, perturb the representation, and assert the invariant that makes the result believable.

slides.label: Recap
slides.notes: Close by returning to the course-wide theme: geometric tools are trustworthy when they connect representation to invariant. Chapter 13 supplies many named algorithms, but the transferable habit is the checklist on the slide. When students meet a new geometry routine, they should ask what it stores, what it tests, how it handles ambiguity, and how to audit the result.
